en: Tiantai Master Zhizhe says:
"At that time, the impoverished son worked for hire," and so forth. This is the second analogy, the meeting of father and son.

It closely leads back to seeing the fire within the Burning House, and distantly leads back to the meaning of the five turbidities within the *Upāya* (Expedient Means) chapter. It is divided into three parts: first, [the son’s arrival].
1. The son’s employment as a laborer corresponds to the fire seen in the "Burning House" parable; the teaching on the Dharma corresponds to the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) seen therein. 2.
The father seeing his son corresponds to the vision of the elder in the "Burning House" parable; it is the vision with the Buddha-eye within the teaching on the Dharma. 3.
The son’s joy and fulfillment of his wishes correspond to the alarm and fear in the "Burning House" parable; it is the arising of the mind of great compassion within the teaching on the Dharma.
In the preceding passage, both the Dharma and the analogy clarify that the father sees the son first; here, it clarifies that the son sees the father first.

From the perspective of the Buddha, his numinous wisdom knows beforehand while the sentient being's capacity subsequently gives rise to a response; thus, it is said that "the father sees the son first.
If one considers the sentient being, there must first be the capacity before there is a response; thus, it is said that "the son sees the father first."

The responsive interaction between the capacity and the response is inconceivable; it neither lags behind nor precedes. Therefore, the preceding and succeeding [moments] are presented interchangeably.
For the sake of textual convenience, I shall now divide this into two sections:
first, the son seeing the father; second, the father seeing the son.
Within these two sections, each is further divided into four parts.
Regarding the first set of four concerning the son seeing his father:
first, the cause for seeing his father, which is the seeking of food and clothing;
Second, he saw his father’s location, situated by the side of the gate;
third, he saw his father’s appearance, seated upon a lion throne;
fourth, he felt fear and avoidance, regretting that he had come here.

Observing the father’s origins—originating from his weariness with suffering and his aspiration for joy, whereby he sought the flavor of principle and gradually accumulated practice until he finally established supramundane roots of goodness—it is therefore said that "he wandered through various forms of labor."
Because these roots of goodness enable one to strike upon the Buddha’s compassion, it is said that "one encounters the father's house.
The father is a metaphor for the Dharmakāya after the realization of the Way, and the house is a metaphor for unconditioned compassion.

Both the great and small capacities simultaneously engage with this dwelling; because there is the great capacity, it is said that "he saw his father from afar," and because there is the small capacity, it is said that "[the son] was staying by the side of the gate."

If there were only the small and no large, one would not see the body of the Honored One with Extraordinary Marks; the father should not have said, "I now have someone to whom my wealth and storehouses may be entrusted.
If there were only the large and no small, he should not have stood by the side of the gate, nor should the son have said, "This is not a place where I obtained goods through hired labor."

The place where one sees the Father is the side of the gate; the two contemplations as skillful means are the two sides of the gate; the capacity within the circle corresponds to the correct view at the center of the gate. Because the Two Vehicles possess only partial truth, they are said to be at the side of the gate; their samādhi of mere emptiness and their partial wisdom-eye merely glance obliquely at the Dharmakāya.

"Seeing his father from afar" involves two kinds of seeing: first, seeing from near; second, seeing from afar. Here, it is said that because the great capacity has only just begun to arise and the act of summoning is distant, it is called "from afar.
Furthermore, because the capacity is subtle and not yet responsive to the response, it is termed "from afar."

Regarding "sitting upon the lion throne": the perfectly retributive Dharma-body dwells securely within the principle of emptiness, free from the two types of delusions—both pervasive and specific—as well as the terrors of the eight māras; therefore, it is said that he sits upon the lion throne.
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra speaks of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), for which the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*) serve as the bed.

Regarding the phrase "a precious footstool supporting the feet": meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are the feet, and the reality of the truths (*satya*) is the stool; thus, the concentration and wisdom of non-arising rely upon the realm of suchness (*tathatā*).
"Brahmin" (婆羅門), formerly translated as "noble and eminent lineage," refers to those from the eighth bhūmi upward.
"Kṣatriya" (剎利) refers to those from the seventh bhūmi downward.
"Householders" refers to those such as the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The older commentaries state that while this sutra elucidates the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is not the eternally abiding Dharma-body; rather, it is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) from another land that is about to manifest in this land, and thus serves as the Dharma-body for this realm, which is why it is surrounded by the various inner ordinary beings.

Now, I say this is not so. If one were to become a Buddha of another direction, then the correspondence between father and son, as well as the relationship between essence and function, attachment and liberation, would all fail to be established, as previously explained.

Furthermore, it would not permit a small-capacity practitioner to strike this [response] while a large-capacity practitioner strikes that; nor should one establish great conditions there while establishing small conditions here, nor should both be established here while both respond there—such a state would result in great confusion.

Now, it is explained that the "Superior Response" (śubha-nirmāṇa-kāya) corresponds to the Bodhisattvas; this is the *vairocana* body of exceptional majesty, which is perceived by those with great spiritual capacities.
The "Inferior Response" corresponds to the followers of the Lesser Vehicle; this is the six-foot-tall body in tattered robes, which is perceived by those with small spiritual capacities.

Now, this sutra clarifies that the eternal *amṛta* (supreme essence) is equal to the *Nirvāṇa*, and that the perfect and sudden *dharmakāya* is equal to the *Avataṃsaka*. The analogy of the elder’s majesty and his retinue, who are surrounded by the respectful attendance of kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas, all points to the retinues within the *Avataṃsaka* without any difference; the characteristics of the Dharma taught here are likewise no different from those elucidated therein.
The Brahmin named Śuddhacārin, noble and pure, is the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāsa-saṃbodhi;
the Kṣatriya refers to the royal lineage, encompassing those from the first bhūmi up to the ninth bhūmi;
the householder, wealthy but not noble, corresponds to the thirty stages of mind (triṃśac-cittotpāda).
“Pearl necklaces” refers to precept, concentration, and wisdom;
together with dharanis and samadhis, these constitute the four necklaces.
“Worth ten million” refers to the merits of the forty stages (bhūmis), which adorn the Dharma-body.

The phrase "officials, commoners, servants, and attendants" clarifies the meaning through different gateways: those who receive the provisional teachings and sever the delusions common to all vehicles are called "commoners," while those who receive the distinct teachings and sever the delusions common to all vehicles are called "officials.
If one clarifies the meaning through the same gateway, these are likewise the provisional *pāramitās*.

Internally, it is identical to true wisdom; externally, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings. This is analogous to the principle where officials and subjects have the duty of internal service and external labor, respectively.
"The white fly-whisk" represents the function of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Regarding "left and right": the right refers to the function of the wisdom that enters emptiness;
it sweeps away the dust of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*). The left refers to the function of the wisdom that enters the provisional (*upāya*);
it sweeps away the dust of ignorance. These two serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that they stand in attendance, and so forth.
"Covered with a precious canopy" refers to true compassion.
"Hanging various flower banners" means that the flowers are the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the banners are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

"Sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground" means pouring down the water of the Dharma to sprinkle the minds of the bodhisattvas, thereby submerging the dust of delusion; it is also the sprinkling of the water of meditative concentration upon the distracted mind.

"Scattering various named flowers" means to spread the seven flowers of purity: namely, purity of precepts (*śīla-viśuddhi*), purity of concentration (*samādhi-viśuddhi*), purity of wisdom (*prajñā-viśuddhi*), purity of the elimination of doubt (*kāṅkṣā-prativinaya-viśuddhi*), purity of the path and what is not the path (*mārgāmārga-jñāna-viśuddhi*), purity of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana-viśuddhi*), and purity of the completion of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā-viśuddhi*). Purity of precepts refers to the three types of ethical discipline, such as the restraint of the senses (*saṃvara-śīla*). Purity of concentration refers to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and others. Purity of wisdom refers to true, ultimate wisdom. Purity of the elimination of doubt refers to having already transcended doubts regarding the two truths. Purity of the path and what is not the path refers to practicing that which is not the path while penetrating the Buddha-way. Purity of knowledge and vision refers to the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) and clearly seeing the Buddha-nature. Purity of the completion of abandonment refers to the accomplishment of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), wherein ignorance is forever exhausted.
"Arraying precious objects" refers to arraying the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
"Entering and exiting as before" and so forth is explained as previously stated.

Regarding "supremely venerable in majestic power," this means that his radiance is boundless and his physical form is boundless; the ocean of his marks is towering and magnificent. This principle must refer to the Buddha Vairocana—how could it possibly refer to any other interpretation?

The section beginning with “The impoverished son saw that his father possessed great power and majesty” constitutes the fourth [section], which concerns seeing the father and fearing him while avoiding him.

Regarding “great power and majesty”: he is called “great power” because his wisdom is vast, and he is called “great majesty” because his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are vast; this is analogous to the meaning of having strength in one’s hands and body as described above.
"Terrified" means that those of small capacity and weak faculties are timid and fearful of the Great Way.

"Regretting having come here" means that the Buddha originally intended to present the Great Dharma to them, but it did not accord with their capacities; they merely harbored the intention of withdrawing from the Great [Vehicle], and thus it is said they regret having come here.

"Privately harboring this thought" means that within their latent dispositions, there was secretly and obscurely such an inclination; it was not that they were openly confronting the Supreme Response Body (Sambhogakāya). Regarding the phrase "or kings, kings, and so forth," Pāpīyas is the "king" and his followers are the "equals.

For those of small capacity who have severed their worldly ties and attained the path of wordless silence, the manifestation of form and image is transcended. Having seen the image of the Supreme Response Body—which is beyond the reach of devas and humans—and having heard the characteristics of the Dharma taught, which are utterly distinct from those of the Two Vehicles, those of meager wisdom and virtue, never having seen or heard such things before, immediately claim, "This is Māra; this is what Māra has spoken."
Briefly opening up the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, Śāriputra harbored doubts, wondering: "Is it not Mara who has become a Buddha to disturb my mind?
If he had initially used the Great [Vehicle] to teach the Small, his suspicion that the Buddha was Mara would have been a fault even today.

Furthermore, "Victorious" (*jina*) should be illustrated by the analogy of a "householder-king" (*gṛhapati-rāja*). The householder represents the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha; therefore, he is the "King. The *dharmakāya* is the teacher of the *saṃbhogakāya*; as the teacher is like a king, many sūtras refer to this [sūtra] as the "King of Sūtras. When wisdom accords with the Dharma, it is said that "wisdom is equal to the Dharma"; thus, the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha is called "Equal" (*sama*). This is the fruit of the Mahāyāna Dharma, not a place where one gains benefit through the Hīnayāna; therefore, it is either the "King" or "Equal to the King."
The phrase "This is not a place where I can obtain goods through hired labor" indicates that those of small capacity cannot receive the great transformation.

The passage from "It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood" up to "where food and clothing are easily obtained" is as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*: "One should be able to deliver these inferior beings by means of the Dharma obtained among the poor."
However, the principle of mere emptiness does not encompass the myriad virtues and is thus not the Tathāgatagarbha; hence it is called a "poor neighborhood.
Because this partial emptiness is suited to those of limited intelligence, it is said that "there is ground upon which to exert effort."

"Food and clothing are easily obtained" means that one is able to obtain the food and clothing of the outflow-free *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*, practicing the giving of robes through one's conduct and the giving of food through one's conduct.
"If I were to dwell here for a long time, I might be oppressed or even forced to work" means that because one practices the Mahāyāna path for immeasurable eons, it is said to be a "long dwelling."
Originally, I was weary of and terrified of birth and death; yet if I were to practice the Mahāyāna, I would inevitably enter into birth and death.
Because I must extensively study the myriad practices, I say that I am being oppressed.
Originally I delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, yet now you compel me to give rise to the Mahāyāna bodhicitta; this is to force me against my will.
Because they abandon the great and take up the small, it is said that they "run swiftly.
From the passage beginning "At that time, the wealthy elder," the second section is the parable of the father seeing his son;
this also has four parts:
First, the father sees his son’s location; second, he recognizes his son upon seeing him; third, he rejoices upon seeing his son; fourth, his wish is fulfilled upon seeing his son.
As for "seeing his son’s location," this refers to the lion throne.
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata dwells in the realm of the ultimate emptiness of fearlessness, clearly illuminating the capacities of sentient beings.
To recognize a child upon merely seeing him means to know that he is a being with whom one has established karmic affinity in the past.

Regarding "the mind is filled with great joy": the Buddha constantly observes his son’s capacity; now that this capacity has arisen in accordance with his compassion, he is therefore joyful. This is precisely the arousal of great compassion upon receiving the teaching of the Dharma. While the burning house represents great terror and alarm, the former refers to the removal of suffering, hence the mention of "terror and alarm," whereas this refers to the bestowing of happiness, hence the mention of "joy."
The phrase "He then thought, 'Now there is someone to whom the treasury may be entrusted'" refers to seeing that his son’s wish has been fulfilled.

Previously, he saw sentient beings fall away from the Great Vehicle and take up the Small Vehicle; like those seeking food in a poor village, they found it difficult to sustain their lives. He constantly desired to give them wealth, but finding no opportunity, he was unable to do so. Today, the opportunity has arrived, coinciding with his heart of great compassion; therefore, he says, "Now there is someone to whom the treasury may be entrusted."

Regarding the phrase "I constantly think of him," this clarifies that it is not merely because he is poor and lacks great wealth; rather, it is because he is oppressed by the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra and is thus pained by [the Bodhisattva’s] great compassion (mahākaruṇā) that he says, "I constantly think of him."
Although one may wish to rescue and deliver others, there are those for whom the conditions are insufficient and who cannot be saved; thus it is said, "there is no means by which I may see them.
Now, however, there are sentient beings whose capacities can be transformed; thus it is said, "and suddenly they come of their own accord."
Because he invokes the mind of great compassion, it is said, "This is most agreeable to my wishes.
The phrase, "Although I am old, I still cherish [this treasure]," explains the reason why his wishes are so well-fulfilled.

Because his transformation of this single lifetime has concluded, he says his years have grown old; yet, having not yet encountered a great capacity for the Dharma, there is no one to whom it may be entrusted—whom will the future disciples follow to attain liberation?
It is for the sake of those who are to be saved that he speaks of his greed and regret.
"Now that the capacity [of the children] has come of its own accord, I have no such anxiety; thus my wish is fulfilled.

The passage "He immediately dispatched attendants to pursue them and bring them back" below clarifies the third analogy of pursuit and enticement. It refers proximately to the abandonment of the couch and the employment of vehicles within the burning house, and distantly to the teaching of the Dharma where the Great [Vehicle] is set aside and the Small [Vehicle] is bestowed.
This passage consists of two parts:
first, sending an attendant in pursuit; second, sending two people to entice him.

Regarding the former pursuit, although those who were physically capable and skilled were available, they were not employed; rather, the general admonition and exhortation in the "Expedient Means" chapter are treated as one unit, while the commentary on the text is divided into three sections.

In the "Burning House" parable, the exhortation to leave and the warning against remaining are each explained in three ways; however, the prose section is abbreviated regarding the instruction to let go. Furthermore, while the long prose combines the exhortation with the warning, the passage on the cessation of the teaching is extensive. In the verses, only the warning is recited and not the exhortation, nor is the cessation of the teaching recited; thus, there are instances of inclusion and omission.
In the prose section of the "Fire House" parable, there are three parts each for the admonition, the exhortation, and the explanation; these are now summarized together.
"He immediately dispatched an attendant to run and seize him" summarizes the preparatory measures of the exhortation gate (*pravartana-mukha*);
"the impoverished son was startled and alarmed" summarizes the lack of receptive capacity (*anadhikāra*) within the exhortation gate.
"Forcefully pulling him back" leads to the appropriateness (*nīya*) of the door of admonition (*śāsana-mukha*);

from "the impoverished son thought to himself that he was innocent" up to "fainting and falling to the ground," it leads to the absence of spiritual capacity (*an-avakāśa*) for the door of admonition.

From "the father saw him from afar" onwards, it collectively leads to the cessation of the teaching (*nivṛtti*) following the door of exhortation (*anuśāsana*). This probes the Buddha’s intention: although the Buddha’s intention regarding the appropriateness of the door of exhortation found no receptive capacity, his purpose was not yet exhausted; he further employed the appropriateness of the door of admonition, and only when this matter could not be helped did he finally cease his teaching.

Regarding the phrase "sending away the peripheral [teachings]," the initial "encouragement gate" (quanmen) refers to what is appropriate for the occasion. Wisdom is that which sends away, while the teaching is that which is sent away; the meaning of principle (liyi) is primary, while the meaning of the teaching (jiaoyi) is peripheral. The Mahāyāna twelvefold canon issued from the Buddha is intended to suit sentient beings; yet there are those who lack the capacity and do not receive it, to whom it is like milk. Therefore, it is said that "the peripheral [teachings] are sent away."

Furthermore, "attendants" refers to ministers, aides, and the like; that is to say, the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas are dispatched to preach the Mahāyāna. For example, in the *Avataṃsaka*, four Bodhisattvas are commanded to explain the forty stages (*bhūmi*); this is precisely what is meant by dispatching attendants.

Regarding the phrase "running swiftly to seize it": the explicit and upright meaning of the Mahāyāna is used to respond to the capacities of beings and hasten toward Bodhi; therefore, it is said in the *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī* that its speed is like the wind.
If one considers the Bodhisattvas to be bystanders, they possess their own supernatural powers and, further empowered by the Buddha, are also able to cause others to swiftly enter Bodhi.
"The impoverished son was startled and alarmed" refers to the absence of receptive capacity (*anadhikāra*) within the gate of exhortation.

Since such a lack of capacity has been manifested, even if he had previously awakened the aspiration, it has long since been abandoned and forgotten; thus, upon finally hearing the Great Teaching, he is startled because it contradicts his own mind and alarmed because he does not recognize it.

Regarding the phrase "crying out and calling out in resentment": in the Hinayana, afflictions are regarded as enemies and birth-and-death as suffering. Thus, if one were to urge that afflictions are themselves bodhi, it would be like crying out and calling it an injustice; if one were to hear that birth-and-death is itself nirvana, it would be like crying out in agony and pain.
"Inanimate things do not receive [the teaching]" refers to the gate of exhortation (*kuan-men*).
Regarding "I do not offend you": since I have made no request, for what purpose do you employ this great transformation to instruct me?
This passage summarizes two points of the gate of exhortation, yet it does not yet summarize the cessation of transformation (*hsi-hua*).
Next, when he is called again but does not come, "holding him more urgently" refers to the instruction on how to lead him [to the gate].
The previous clarification regarding the exhortation to do good was still a matter of leisure; now, saying "I shall explain for you matters of fear" constitutes the urgency.
Although it says "forcibly pulling them back," this is a warning with bitter words intended to make them distance themselves from evil.
Since there is no internal capacity [for awakening] yet they are externally constrained by the Great Transformation, this is precisely what is meant by "forcibly pulling them back."
"Thinking of oneself as being without fault" refers to the gate of receiving and not receiving admonitions.

"Fault" here means compassion; because sentient beings have faults, they enter the prison of birth and death, and Bodhisattvas likewise enter the prison due to their faults. Those of the Two Vehicles lack great compassion, and thus they are said to be "without fault."

To cause one to enter the cycle of birth and death is itself to be imprisoned; if one enters birth and death without great skillful means, one will inevitably and forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles, and is therefore said to be "certainly dead."
Reflecting on these matters, it is said that they become "even more terrified.
Because they are compelled by the Great Teaching while their limited wisdom cannot comprehend it, it is said that they "faint away."

They immediately give rise to slander and will surely fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, it is said they "fall to the ground," which also signifies being bewildered and drowning in the ground of ignorance.
From the passage "The father sees him from afar" is the third stage: he relinquishes his exhortations and ceases his Mahāyāna transformation.
This consists of four parts:

first, contemplating the cessation of transformation; second, explaining the cessation of transformation; third, the correct cessation of transformation; and fourth, the appropriate application of the cessation of transformation.
Initially there were two considerations:
first, knowing that those with great aspirations are weak; second, knowing that those with small aspirations are strong.

Regarding the phrase "the father saw from afar": because the child was far removed from the father, it is called "afar"; because he is a child for whom the father has established a karmic connection, it is said that he "saw" him.

Regarding the phrase "and spoke to the messenger": if we take the teaching as the messenger, it means that wisdom is fundamentally what expounds the teaching; when wisdom perceives there is no receptive capacity (*indriya*), wisdom ceases, and thus the teaching ceases.

If we take the person as the messenger, it means speaking to the various Bodhisattvas that they need not manifest their honored and wondrous bodies for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles. This is the meaning found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states: "Restrain the fragrance of your body so that those sentient beings do not give rise to deluded attachments," and also in the case of Samantabhadra entering this Sahā world, who contracts his body to make it small. All such instances share this same principle.
Regarding "Do not force him to come": since he lacks the great capacity [for the teaching], one fears it might damage his roots of goodness; therefore, it says "do not force.
In my private view, "There is no need for this person" refers to the application of the method of ceasing exhortation through contemplation;
"Do not force him to come" refers to the application of the method of ceasing admonition through contemplation.

"Sprinkling cold water on the face" refers to the second [stage]: knowing that one’s aspirations are still minor, one should employ ash to sever the principle [of attachment] and use water to remove the heat of view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusion (*saṃjñā-kleśa*).
"Face" means that one loathes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which is called the "back," and turns toward *nirvāṇa* as if facing it directly.
“Awakening” means that by opening the small capacity of the disciples, they attain liberation from vexation and delusion and realize the Four Noble Truths.
“Do not speak with them again” means that one must certainly cease the teaching of the Mahāyāna.

"From 'For what reason? onwards is the second section, which explains the intention for ceasing the transformation [of the teaching]. It is because [the Buddha] himself felt weary of suffering and delighted in emptiness, yet was intimately familiar with those of inferior capacity and lacked compassion; thus, he feared the Great Dharma would be difficult to propagate and temporarily allowed them to follow their lesser inclinations. This suppressed the Buddha’s original intent, which is why he ceased his transformative activity."

He clearly understood that the two trillion Buddhas who had previously inspired him toward the Way were not entirely devoid of great potential; thus, he temporarily ceased his grand transformation, for the Buddha’s intention was not yet fulfilled, awaiting a later occasion.

Regarding the phrase "not speaking of others": in the former teachings of the Hīnayāna, one spoke according to the intentions of others as a skillful means of concealment, calling oneself a śrāvaka; one did not speak according to one's own intention, claiming to be a bodhisattva.
"Below the passage 'The messenger spoke to him,' the third section correctly clarifies the cessation of the great transformation.

'I now release you' indicates that he knew the capacity for the Great [Vehicle] was weak; 'you may go wherever you wish' indicates that he knew the power of their minor goodness was strong. Due to these two conditions, he ceased his great transformation."
"From 'The impoverished son rejoices' onwards is the fourth section, which describes the cessation of the teaching in accordance with the capacities of the audience.
Because they were no longer coerced by the Great Teaching, they "rejoiced";
because they avoided the grave sin of slandering the Dharma and were spared from the three miserable realms, it says "from the ground."
Because a small measure of wholesome goodness has arisen, it is said that he "arises.

Furthermore, previously he was suited for the Great Dharma, yet he lay bewildered and unable to understand upon the ground of ignorance; now, by being provided with the Small [Vehicle], he may attain awakening, and thus it is said that he "rises from the ground."
Because one seeks the Dharma of the Path within the Four Noble Truths, it is said that "he goes to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing";
or because one seeks the Path among the four views, it is called the "poor quarters."
The section beginning with "Intending to entice" refers to the secret dispatching of two individuals to entice [the children]; this has two parts:
first, the teaching of equality, which near-term leads by employing the three vehicles to save the children, and far-term leads back to the provisional means bestowed at Vārāṇasī;

second, from "Furthermore, on another day" onwards, taking the underlying intent, it leads back to the fact that the Dharma-body has long illuminated these skillful means—it was not only upon reaching the Bodhi tree that he first knew to employ them small-scale. Having early on discerned sentient beings, he brought about the difficulty of being intimately familiar with the soiled robes of the Honored One’s special manifestation; therefore, he now traces back to previous events to establish the present understanding.
Question:
For what reason were the four great disciples able to know that the Dharma-body has long been shining?
Answer:

By inferring the near to know the distant, we see that had he initially perceived at the Bodhi tree that there were no beings of great capacity, he would not have descended from Tuṣita, entrusted his sublime wisdom to a womb, or even manifested the presence of afflictions by taking a consort and fathering a son; nor would he have severed the fetters with the thirty-four moments of mind, thereby realizing liberation. Thus, we verify that after casting off the subtle necklace of the ocean of marks of a Great Man, he has long since donned the coarse and tattered robes of the six-foot form.
Now, first, let us explain the teaching of the Equalization.
Regarding "guiding," there are four sections in the text of the "Parable Chapter":

first, employing skillful means to adapt to the capacity; second, knowing their prior inclinations; third, praising the three vehicles; and fourth, fulfilling their respective wishes. There are likewise four [sections] in the "Expedient Means Chapter."
Now there are also four summary statements (*piṇḍārtha*).
From "He was about to entice him" onwards is the summary of the preceding section on the provisional suitability.

"At that time, the two messengers immediately sought the impoverished son and, having found him," summarizes the preceding section on knowing that the son’s prior mind possessed the latent capacity (*gotra*).
"Relating the aforementioned matters" refers to receiving the praise above regarding the rarity of the three vehicles.
"The impoverished son first takes his payment," and so forth, refers to the fulfillment of the aforementioned wish to hasten out of the burning house.

First, regarding "intending to entice and lead": since the great transformation has already ceased and it would be improper to abandon them alone, he wishes to establish skillful means; thus, he says "intending.
Regarding "secretly dispatching two people": as the four disciples each led their own respective groups and did not involve the bodhisattvas, he says "two people."

In terms of the Dharma, this refers to the four truths of dependent origination; in terms of principle, it refers to the constructed (saṃskṛta) and the ultimate (paramārtha) within the conventional and ultimate; in terms of persons, it refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Initially, in the Mahāyāna context, it was said that "a bystander is secretly sent away" to symbolize the one ultimate truth, the one Mahāyāna teaching, and the one bodhisattva person. Now, clarifying the skillful means (upāya), the concealment of the ultimate is termed "secret," and the pointing toward the partial truth is termed "sending away."
Regarding the teaching, the full syllables (*pūrṇākṣara*) are concealed and thus termed "secret," while the half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*) are pointed out as being "expelled.
Regarding the person, it is called "secret" because he internally maintains the practices of a bodhisattva, and it is called "expelled" because he externally manifests as a śrāvaka.

"Form" refers to the fact that within the teachings of the Two Vehicles, one does not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana), but instead preaches only suffering, impermanence, and impurity; this is precisely what is meant by "the appearance of the body being haggard."
In terms of individuals, the various bodhisattvas conceal their original nature and manifest provisional forms.
This is not a definitive teaching; because they lack the ten powers and the fearlessnesses, they are said to be "without majestic virtue."
The phrase "you may go to him" refers to employing the Small Teaching (Hīnayāna) for those of small capacity.
Because the Great Teaching clarifies principles that are direct and substantial, it says "run quickly to seize him";
because the Small Teaching clarifies principles that are circuitous and obscure, it says "speak slowly."
Regarding the phrase "this is the place of practice," the two paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are the places for the practice of severing delusions.

Regarding the phrase "I shall give you double the price": the five precepts and ten wholesome acts merely enable one to escape the three miserable realms; now, the Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can bring about transcendence from birth and death—this constitutes the first multiple.

Furthermore, the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress delusions, whereas practicing the Four Noble Truths can actually sever delusions and lead to *nirvāṇa*—this constitutes the second multiple.
Regarding the phrase "if the impoverished son consents," consent refers to the presence of spiritual capacity (*indriya*), which entails the establishment of the teaching;
lack of consent refers to the absence of such capacity, in which case the teaching is not established.

Regarding the question "what does he wish to do?"—those of the Two Vehicles desire only to eliminate delusions and attain realization, without concern for purifying Buddha-lands or bringing sentient beings to maturity.

The reason it is said, "I hire you to remove the filth; we two shall work together as well," is that those of the Two Vehicles, possessing dull faculties, must rely on the teachings to practice before they can cultivate their karma. In terms of principle, this refers to the mutual support between wisdom and the truths (*satya*); in terms of persons, it refers to the provisional person practicing together with the real person.

Regarding the phrase, "At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son": secondly, because they have thoroughly discerned that there is a latent capacity [for awakening], it is said "they have already found him"; this takes up the previous point regarding their knowledge of his prior disposition.
"Having fully related the aforementioned matters," below, is the third section: the narration of the hiring of laborers, which leads into the praise of the three vehicles mentioned above.
One removes the filth of suffering and its origin, and takes the price of the path and its cessation.

"First the impoverished son takes the wages and immediately proceeds to remove the filth"—this fourth section, "immediately proceeding to perform the work," refers to fulfilling the aforementioned wishes and vying to escape from the burning house.
The followers of the Two Vehicles aspire to the fruit and practice the cause; thus, they take [the fruit] first.

As for the phrase, "The father saw his sons and felt pity and wonder," he was amazed that they did not seek the Buddha-way, and he pitied them for taking the stage of Arhatship—what they lose is great while what they gain is meager—and therefore he spoke of his wonder.
This concludes the text summarizing the meaning of the parable.

From the passage beginning with "Furthermore, on another day" onwards is the second section: the summary of the underlying intent. This refers to how primordial wisdom first illuminates [the truth], having long ago established skillful means and followed [beings] through difficult circumstances; it is not as if the causal conditions were only perceived beneath the tree, as was explained above.
This passage consists of four parts:
first, "On another day," which indicates that he had long intended to employ provisional wisdom to provide an appropriate teaching;
second, seeing his son's emaciated state, which shows that he had long known the skillful means to be used as a means of attraction.
Third, having been liberated from the sublime and attached to the coarse, they have long known that they must sigh for the three vehicles;
fourth, the father personally instructs his sons to act, and having long known this, they now receive and practice it according to their wishes—this is the first [of these points].
The word "furthermore" (*yòu*) is a term used for emphasis.

As he intends to grasp the underlying meaning and lead [beings] to the ground of the Dharma-body, knowing long since the capacities of those of great and small faculties and bestowing transformation through the principles of one and three, he reiterates the Buddha’s intent; thus, he marks this section with the character "furthermore."

"Another day" (*tārā*) refers to the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) considering their own skillful means as "self" and the teachings of the two vehicles as "other"; this refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

"Day" (*rā*) signifies time, and it also signifies wisdom (*jñāna*). Because one employs wisdom to illuminate the capacities [of beings] according to the time of the Dharma-body, it is called "another day."
According to this principle, true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) illuminating reality is taken as "self," while expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna) illuminating skillful means is taken as "other.

Within the framework of the teachings, that which leads one to comprehend the activities of the nirmāṇakāya is designated as the day of "self," whereas that which does not involve the activities of the nirmāṇakāya is designated as the day of "other."

If we consider it in relation to the Tathāgata, his own practice of the wisdom of means and reality is all termed "self," while the Tathāgata’s illumination of the means and reality for the sake of transforming others is all termed "other."
The Tathāgata’s illumination of both the provisional and the real for himself and others consists of illuminating the real for himself and illuminating the provisional for others.

At the time of this realization and mastery of the Dharmakāya, he employs the provisional wisdom that transforms others to illuminate whether the provisional capacities [of beings] exist or not, and to illuminate whether the provisional activities [of transformation] are appropriate or not; since all these are illuminated by provisional wisdom, they are referred to as "for others."

If one understands according to this meaning, one comprehends the provisional matters of transforming others through the teachings; thus, while the Two Vehicles refer to their own affairs, they explore and comprehend the provisional means for both themselves and others. Since these provisional means are not the affairs of the Two Vehicles, they are termed "other."

Although there are two interpretations, both will be established later; for now, following the realization of the Two Vehicles and tracking the text regarding "another day," we shall explore how their realization apprehends the illumination of sentient beings within the Dharmakāya.
Regarding "the window," partial vision is limited; this symbolizes how expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminates those with partial capacities.
Regarding "remote," because the small is far removed from the great and hangs at a great distance, it is called "remote."

Regarding the phrase "seeing the child": in the past, he planted the seeds of what is called a "great reputation" as a son; because he modeled himself after the Great [Vehicle], it is said that he "saw" [the child].
Since the window and door were narrow and constricted, they were not yet suitable for the Great Transformation; therefore, he suspended the Great and applied the Small.
Below the term "emaciated" (*karśa*), the second [point] concerns the prior knowledge that there are minor diversions.

Having little power from cultivating the causes is "emaciated" (*karśa*); having little power from cultivating the causes of merit is "lean" (*kṛśa*). Internally fearing impermanence is "withered" (*tāpa*); externally encountering the eight sufferings is "dejected" (*paritāpa*).
The four stages of abiding are "filth and earth," and ignorance is "dust and grime.
From "immediately casting off the necklaces" onwards is the third section, in which the Leader, knowing that [the children] must be exhorted, praises the rarity of the three vehicles.
To cast off the wondrous robes is a metaphor for the concealment of the immeasurable merits of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

The "necklaces" consist of the forty-two stages, as well as morality, concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇīs*; the "fine, soft upper garments" are the patience of tranquil extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*); and the "ornaments" are the ocean of major and minor marks.

If his appearance and robes were magnificent, the sons [of the Buddha] would be startled and fearful; the followers of the Two Vehicles should not behold such marks and signs of excellence, and for this reason he removed them.

As for "putting on coarse and tattered [clothes]," appearing in a sixteen-foot form is "coarse," while the patience toward beings (*sattvā-kṣānti*) and the patience regarding dharmas (*dharma-kṣānti*) are "tattered."
"His body covered in dust and soil" refers to the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and outflows (*āsrava*).

"Holding a dustpan for cleaning filth" and below refers only to the treatment of the tainted dharmas of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); it does not concern the pure wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

The left hand symbolizes reality (śūnyatā), and the right hand symbolizes skillful means (upāya). Skillful means are easy to employ; by means of this dharma, one severs the fetters to become a Buddha, and further employs it to transform others.
The phrase "appearing to have fear" indicates that he manifests the same dread of birth and death, as well as the retributions of the cold wind and the horse-barley.

From the passage "He spoke to the laborers" onwards is the fourth section, which uses the analogy of personally instructing his sons; this refers to the seven categories of the Dharma-gates within the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (the *Dōhin*), used to manifest the aspect of removing dung—that is, leading the aforementioned sons, whose minds are each courageous and sharp, pushing one another and racing together in competition to escape the burning house.
First, the analogy of the hired laborer illustrates the four foundations of mindfulness as the stage of the external ordinary person;
second, the analogy of urging diligence and not allowing laxity illustrates the four right efforts;
third, the phrase "Ho there, man! and the injunction not to go elsewhere illustrates the four bases of psychic power.
4. From "Take care to settle your mind" onwards is called the analogy of consolation, which illustrates the five faculties (*pañcendriya*);
5. From "Why is that? onwards is called the analogy of being free from the five faults, which illustrates the five powers (*pañcabala*).
The preceding four lines constitute the second stage of the inner ordinary person (*prthagjana*).
Sixth, the immediate metaphor of the elder naming [the son] as his own child illustrates the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Seventh, from "Although he rejoices at this encounter" onwards, the teaching regarding the constant command to remove filth illustrates the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
These two lines constitute the third stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Now, regarding the initial address to "all laborers," this refers to the teaching of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) to demonstrate the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); for these are the vessels for removing filth and the spheres for severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The *Śālistamba-sūtra* (or *Upadeśa*) states: "By constantly practicing the path in reliance upon the foundations of mindfulness, one can destroy the four inversions. To grasp this and apply it with courageous vigor within the burning house is precisely what constitutes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).

Second, "do not become lax" means to cause one to diligently cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If one becomes lax, one cannot eliminate the two evils nor give rise to the two virtues. By means of the two types of diligence, one can ignite the fire of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*), push and pull against the burning house, and enter the stage of the warmth of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of skillful means one comes near to that son": although the mind has not yet been warmed by the fire of principle through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it remains distant and cannot be approached; however, once the skillful means of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) are first attained, one may then approach it.

Third, regarding "Ho! Man": "Ho" is both an exclamation of awakening and a reproach. In the aforementioned right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), agitation is itself the factor of wisdom (*prajñā-dharma*). Just as a man is of masculine nature, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are factors of concentration (*samādhi-dharma*); whereas a woman is of feminine nature, because right effort involves such exertion and cannot correspond with true reality, it is therefore called out with a startled reproach to cause one to abandon distraction and enter stillness; thus, it says, "Ho! Man."

Regarding the phrase "You should always practice this and not go elsewhere": if mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) are not focused and one-pointed, they are not called "constant. Among the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), concentration does not shift its object; thus, when one contemplates, there is concentration, and when one contemplates, there is cessation. Because concentration and cessation are one-pointed, it is "constant," and because it is not distracted or disturbed, "do not go elsewhere."
This still occurs within the process of mutual pushing and shoving, which corresponds to the stage of the "Summits" (mūrdhāna-dharma).

Regarding the phrase "I shall increase your price": within the mental contemplation of the "Heat" (uṣmagata-dharma) stage, one cannot yet give rise to the truth; however, because one can give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava) state within the mental contemplation [of the Summits], it is said that the price is increased.

If there is anything required—whether outflow-tainted or outflow-free, wholesome, auxiliary to the path, or the direct path—all may be sought through the contemplation of "as one wishes," and whatever is desired is immediately obtained.

The essence of the four dhyānas contains a forest of factors like a basin; the emptiness of persons is coarse like rice, while the emptiness of phenomena is subtle like flour; this is the direct path.
The sixteen contemplations on the Four Truths—wherein impermanence is like salt and suffering is like vinegar—are the aids to the Path (*mārga*).
Just as rice and flour are difficult to eat and must be mixed with salt and vinegar, so too is the True Path difficult to manifest and requires the assistance of the aids to the Path.

Regarding the phrase "Do not harbor self-doubt or difficulty": this concludes the preceding discussion on the primary and auxiliary practices. It instructs one not to doubt because [the goal] is definitively present within the *yirui guan* (contemplation of accordance with one's wishes); it says "do not find it difficult" because one should maintain the thought that [the goal] can certainly be accomplished as if it were one's own possession.

Regarding the phrase "there are also aged and infirm messengers": if one wishes to directly employ the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to act as hands and feet for the sake of driving and employing others, such powers are also present within the contemplations according to one's will; however, these powers are weak and inferior, their function being similar to that of aged and infirm messengers who, though not robust, are still capable of labor.

Furthermore, when seeking the principle through the Right Path, the Right Path is weak and has not yet been able to manifest the Truth; thus, one requires the assistance of the auxiliary paths, such as the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the ten notions (*daśasaṃjñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

Regarding "assisting those who practice the Way," this method is also present within the contemplation of *yathābhūta* (things as they truly are). If one obtains assistance that aids what is correct, one immediately becomes a person of shared liberation.
Fourth, "wishing to settle the mind in peace" means attaining the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) so that they are firm, stable, and difficult to destroy.

“I am like your father” means that because his patience and understanding are adjacent to the ultimate truth yet remain semblances rather than the reality itself, he says he is “like a father,” and is likewise “like a son.
“Do not worry further” means to cause him to set his mind at ease so as to destroy [the afflictions of] views and thoughts.

Fifth, regarding "I am old and you are young": the Buddha, having reached the end of the path, is fully endowed with wisdom and abandonment; thus he is called "old. You, being at the beginning of the path, do not yet possess wisdom and abandonment; thus you are called "young and vigorous. This refers to the stage of the Dharma of Patience (*kṣānti*).
To be free from the five faults means to attain the five powers and thereby distance oneself from the five unwholesome dharmas.

Because one attains the power of faith, one does not deceive; because of the power of diligence, one does not become indolent; because of the power of mindfulness, one does not give rise to anger; because of the power of concentration, one does not harbor resentment; and because of the power of wisdom, one does not utter words of complaint.

"Other practitioners" refers, distantly, to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who are called "other practitioners" because they seek the truth through various views; it refers, proximately, to those in the four stages beginning with *ūṣmagata*, who are also called "other practitioners" because they have not yet escaped the five faults.
This text is free from the five faults; it refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*). Regarding the phrase "from now on, like a son born [to one's parents]":

the duration of the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) consists of sixteen moments (*kṣaṇa*), which is still relatively long; although the stage of middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*) contracts the contemplation, it is not yet a single moment. However, the stage of upper patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) is the final moment of the mundane state, where the mind is adjacent to the truth and close to the noble ones (*ārya*); therefore, this stage is called "like a son born," which is the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Sixth, regarding the phrase "Immediately the elder further gave him a name, calling him 'Son'": because he has attained the Eightfold Right Path and is racing forward together with others within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), he is said to be named "Son."

Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is not distant from the Truth, it is said to be "immediate. The *Āgama* speaks of five kinds of sons of the Buddha: those in the four fruits of the path and the pratyekabuddha are called true sons of the Buddha; as for the bodhisattva, who has not severed the fetters, the meaning of being a "son" is not yet established.

"Then, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter," and so forth, is the seventh analogy: the analogy of being constantly employed as a laborer. Although he is the son, his contemplation is not yet complete;

he still dwells in the stage of training (śaikṣa) and has not attained the state beyond difficulty (asaṃskṛta). Therefore, for twenty years he is constantly made to remove filth, and he likewise knows for himself that he is not fit to succeed to the great estate. This is precisely the exhaustion of suffering through practicing according to the teaching; hence it says, "He still calls himself a lowly hired laborer."

If one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna) feels weary of the lesser vehicle and aspires to the greater, and the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened, then one should immediately bestow the Mahāyāna upon them; furthermore, it is not necessary to advance further to sever the remaining residual fetters. This is precisely because if one does not abandon the lesser aspiration, the great capacity will not be awakened. For this reason, they are made to exhaust their outflows by relying on the teachings for the time being; thus it is said: "For this reason, for twenty years he constantly had him remove filth."
Regarding the phrase "twenty years": for one who has seen the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya), there is one liberation and one unhindered knowledge;
for one who practices through cultivation (bhāvanā), there are nine unhindered knowledges and nine liberations; therefore, it is said to be "twenty years."
Furthermore, it is said that severing the fetters through the two paths of vision and cultivation is called "twenty years.
It is also said that the five lower-tier and five upper-tier fetters constitute these twenty years.
It is further stated that because one has severed the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) within the teachings of the Two Vehicles, it is called "twenty years.
It is also stated that because one relies on the two messengers to jointly sever the remaining fetters (*anuśaya*), it is called "twenty years."

Because he came to evoke the Buddha due to the capacity for the two vehicles, it is said: "Since you, my son, first came, twenty years have already passed. If one abides in the stage of the two vehicles while turning the Mahāyāna teaching, this is called "managing the household affairs for twenty years."
Each of these twenty phrases has its own specific significance; pointing to this single phrase refers to the stage of escaping the burning house of the triple world.

The section beginning with "After this" constitutes the fourth analogy, that of entrusting the family estate: it proximately refers to the bestowing of the great vehicle within the analogy of the burning house, and distantly refers to the unsurpassed path within the discourse on the Dharma.
This consists of two parts:
first, the summary; second, the entrustment.

Each of these further comprises two sub-sections, together encompassing the four intentions regarding the burning house and the granting of the carts, which are also the four intentions for revealing the reality [of the One Vehicle] in the "Expedient Means" chapter.
The first chapter has two parts:
first, "mutual trust in the nature of the mind," which refers to receiving the exemption from calamity;
second, "entrusting him with the family business" so that he gradually attains prosperity and fulfills his great aspiration, which refers to requesting the vehicle.
The two points in the subsequent chapter are:
first, the entrustment of the family estate, which refers to receiving the gift of the great chariot;
second, the joy of having received the entrustment, which refers to the delight upon receiving the aforementioned chariot.

Because of his mental disposition and trustworthiness, he was entrusted with the family business; once he had become thoroughly familiar with and fully understood the business, he achieved great ambition. Because his will was sound and robust, he was granted the family business; having been granted the business, he was filled with joy. Since there are distinctions between the distant and the near, if one were not first taught manual labor and provided with a day’s wage, how could one’s character be trusted to entrust him with the business and the wealth?

Internally, he attained realization through the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and severed his fetters; thus, he was capable of hearing the *Mahāsāṃnipāta-sūtra*, receiving the refutation [of views] in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and turning the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* until he was entrusted with the Dharma-treasure.
One should know that receiving wages for labor is the remote cause, while entrusting one's affairs based on trust is the proximate cause.
Furthermore, within the preceding analogy of the inducement, there is a sequential reception beginning from the Bodhi tree and ending with the departure from the house;
there is also a comprehensive reception beginning from the Dharma-body and ending with the exhaustion of all thought.

Now, there are also two types of leading: the initial leading, which probes the four stages of compassion to bring beings to maturity; and the final leading, which entrusts the Dharma-treasure to reach the ultimate single flavor. When the distant and near, the beginning and the end, are discussed together, they constitute the five flavors.

What does this mean? It refers to sending aside a bystander; what the bystander says serves as an analogy for the *Avataṃsaka*’s Perfect and Sudden teaching. This teaching is the very first; the bystander is likened to the cow, and what he says is likened to the milk. Internally, this corresponds to the twelve divisions of the sūtras emerging from the Buddha, which is the "first flavor. When this is presented to those of the Two Vehicles, they lack the capacity to receive it and, becoming bewildered and distressed, fall to the ground. To their entire life, it is like the flavor of milk.

Next, the secret dispatching of two people to explain the method of removing filth is clarified; this is a metaphor for the teaching of the Three Vehicles at the Deer Park after the cessation of the Great [Vehicle]. Within the Small Vehicle, it refers to faith transforming the ordinary person into a sage, like the transformation of milk into curd. Internally, it corresponds to the production of the *sūtras* from the twelve divisions of scripture, which is the second flavor.

Next, it is explained that the mind’s characteristics allow for the realization of the essence, such that entering and emerging [from the teachings] is without difficulty. This is illustrated by the period following the Tripiṭaka, when the Vaipulya sūtras were preached and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* was propagated to subvert the Great [Vehicle] and elevate the Small. When those of the Two Vehicles heard the Great, they did not slander it; when the Small was subverted, they did not regress. This is truly because, through the Tripiṭaka, they had severed their fetters and obtained the "price of a single day," and thus were permitted to freely praise or criticize. Had they not yet severed their fetters, they would have been incapable of hearing the elevation of the Great, just as they previously could not accept the gates of exhortation; nor would they have been capable of hearing the subversion of the Small, just as they previously could not accept the gates of admonition. That they now neither slander nor regress is due to their realizing and believing the characteristics of the mind.

Once the parents have personally realized the Lesser Vehicle, they will believe that the Great Vehicle is not false; having obtained the price of Nirvana, their bodies are broken [by suffering] yet they do not give rise to anger. Although it is not their own affair, they do not doubt or slander it. This mind is pure and mature, like clarified butter produced from curd; internally, it corresponds to the emergence of the Vaipulya Sutras from the Sūtras—this is the third flavor.

Next, the passage beginning with "The elder knew for himself that he would soon die" illustrates how, after [the sons] have gained mutual trust and entered and exited [the house] without difficulty, they are entrusted with the family business and made to receive the teachings by expounding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* as great bodhisattvas. Having taken charge of the various goods and mastered the gateway of the Dharma, their minds become clear and their eloquence increases, leading them to cherish and delight in it all the more. They only regret dwelling in the Lesser Vehicle, which is not their rightful portion; if they were further permitted to transcend it, would they not be joyful? Thereupon, their minds gradually become open and expansive, and they fulfill their great aspiration—just as fresh butter (*navanīta*) emerges from clarified butter (*ghṛta*). This is the emergence of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* from the Vaipulya (Equally Extensive) teachings; it is the fourth flavor.

Next, regarding the phrase "when about to pass away, he summons his son": this is a metaphor for the period following *prajñā*, wherein the natural disposition is determined and the father-son relationship is established; it refers to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which unifies the three vehicles into one, entrusts the treasury, and bestows the prediction of enlightenment. It reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and demonstrates the true aspect, whereby the doubts of the bodhisattvas are removed and the śrāvakas become Buddhas—all being brought to nirvāṇa by means of the Tathāgata’s own nirvāṇa. This is like extracting *sarpirmaṇḍa* (clarified butter) from matured *ghṛta*; it is the Great Nirvāṇa emerging from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and is thus the fifth flavor.

The four great disciples deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent; they explored and received the teachings of his one transformation through its five flavors, and the sequence from beginning to end is set forth here in this text.
The text concerning the reception of the family legacy is twofold:
first, the mutual trust in the essential nature; second, the command to receive the legacy.

Regarding the two aspects of "believing according to the substance" (*tǐ-xìn*), first is the clarification of believing according to the substance; here, both [father and son] still occupy their original positions.

Now, concerning the first aspect, "mutual belief" (*hùxiāng-xìn*): this refers to the fact that within the Tripitaka, one has obtained the price of Nirvana, which is not false; now, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, this Mahayana is taught, and it likewise is not false. This is precisely the son believing the father.

The Buddha, knowing that these individuals had already severed their views and afflictions and would certainly not slander what they heard, understood that because their untainted faculties were sharp, even hearing a subtle teaching would give rise to faith; this is like a father’s faith in his son.
Because of this, seeing the *vairocana-kāya* (the markless body) and hearing the Mahāyāna teachings is called "entering";

yet, being further rebuked and corrected, they still see the sixteen-foot body preaching the Hīnayāna dharma, which is called "exiting. Thus, there is no doubt or difficulty regarding this entering and exiting through the Great and Small Vehicles.

Second, regarding the phrase "yet he still remains in his original place": although he enters and exits [the state of meditative concentration] without difficulty and hears the Mahāyāna, he claims that this is the business of a bodhisattva and not within the scope of his own wisdom; thus, he is unwilling to turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great, remaining as an arhat and not saying that he will become a Buddha in the future. This refers to the teaching of the *Mahāsannipāta*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Sūtra on the Birth of Ghee*. From the passage in the World-Honored One’s discourse concerning the illness of the elder, down to the second point where the family business is entrusted to him, this refers to the teaching of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*—the "Ripe Ghee"—where the Buddha commands him to turn and teach the *Prajñā*.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the command to oversee household affairs; second, the acceptance of the command and the taking of charge.
Each of these two chapters is further divided into four sections.

Regarding the first four points: first, clarifying the proper timing; second, maintaining a correct livelihood and attending to household affairs; third, admonishing them to embody my intent; and fourth, commanding that nothing be lost or neglected.

Initially, regarding the phrase "before long he will die": when the conditions for existence arise, one responds by being born; when the conditions are exhausted, one should withdraw and pass away, which is death. Now that the transformative conditions are nearing their end, his passing is not far off.
"Speaking to the poor son, [the father] says, 'I now have much... and so forth, is the second section, commanding him to manage the household affairs.

"Gold" refers to the principle of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), and "silver" refers to the principle of the Shared Teaching (Tong-jiao). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that the True Truth does not transcend these two; yet, when it says "much," this is because while the principle itself is not manifold, it can be described as manifold in terms of its various gateways. For example, emptiness is not eighteen in itself, yet it is called the "eighteen kinds of emptiness" based on its negation of the eighteen dharmas.
Within the "Exhortation to Study," it is clarified that all dharma-gates are precious treasures.
"Granary" refers to the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely the one hundred and eight samādhis;
"Warehouse" refers to the gates of wisdom (*prajñā*), namely the sphere of the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The storehouses of both the general and specific types of concentration and wisdom contain all meditative absorptions and insights without deficiency; because they are filled within and overflow without, it is said that they are "replete and overflowing."
Regarding the phrase "to what extent," when speaking of *prajñā*, there are two gates: the extensive and the concise.

A bodhisattva practicing *prajñā* should understand these concise and extensive characteristics: the concise is "less" and the extensive is "more"; practicing for oneself is "taking," while transforming others is "giving."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "You should speak for the sake of the bodhisattvas," which is why it says, "You know them all.
The section beginning with "My mind is thus" constitutes the third part: the admonition on the essence.
Regarding "my mind": the Buddha takes Prajñā as his mind; you who now transmit the lamp should speak in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.

Furthermore, as for those of the Two Vehicles whose fundamental understanding is the emptiness of analytical dharma (prajñapti-śūnyatā), when it says "you must embody this meaning," it means that you are commanded to transform your teaching so that they may likewise embody the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-nairātmya) as I do.

In the past, when I was commanded to transmit the lamp to others, I now realize that the Buddha intended for me to recognize the gateway to the essence; therefore, he said, "You should embody this meaning."
Regarding the statement, "Now I and you are indeed not different," there are three ways to explain this:
first, that he was empowered to teach so that his teaching is not different from the Buddha's;

second, that they are not different when considered from the perspective of principle (*tattva*), because all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); and third, that Subhūti’s suchness and the Tathāgata’s suchness are a single suchness without a second suchness, and thus it is said they are indeed not different.

Third, regarding the present time: one now realizes for the first time that the natural affinity between father and son is fundamentally no different [from that of others], whereas those of the Two Vehicles merely claimed they were granted a distinct [spiritual] empowerment.
"You should apply yourself with diligence" and below constitutes the fourth point: the command not to allow this to be lost or neglected.

"You must expound the Prajñā teachings for the sake of the bodhisattvas so that they are not lost; secondly, from the perspective of principle, this is your own dharma which you shall need to employ at a later time, and for that reason, you must ensure it is not lost."
"Immediately receiving the instruction" below marks the second section, Receiving the Mandate.
This is further divided into four parts:
first, formally receiving the mandate and taking it to heart.
2. "Lack of aspiration for attainment": Although Subhūti preaches the Prajñāpāramitā, he says of himself, "I have no share in this. 3.

"Not yet having abandoned the inferior mind and still remaining in one's original station": This refers to those abiding in the stage of an Arhat; although they may aspire to the Great Vehicle, they have not yet definitively declared their intent to become Bodhisattvas.

"Not yet having abandoned the inferior mind": Although they may feel shame for the Small Vehicle, they have not yet definitively declared that they will relinquish the realization of the Small Vehicle.

4. "After a short time, the father knew his son's intention," and so forth, refers to the parable of requesting the vehicle mentioned above; it signifies that [the son] has come to despise his former mind and desires to seek the Great Way, as the great capacity [for enlightenment] has been awakened.
Question:
When is it called "a short time"?
Answer:

One interpretation states that after the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* was concluded, he traveled and observed elsewhere, reflecting upon the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates he had mastered; as he pondered whether his realization was lost or preserved, and so forth, such reflections were precisely the moment when the capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened.
At this time, because it was not long since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that "not much time had passed.
Furthermore, when the *Anantārthika* (The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings) was being expounded, the spiritual capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened. How is this known?
Within the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, seven kinds of skillful means are elucidated, wherein immeasurable gradual and sudden teachings arise from a single Dharma.

Having heard this teaching, one reflects that the three baskets and the three vehicles of the past all likewise arise from this single Dharma; thus, these three vehicles should also enter into the One. When one contemplates in this way, the mind gradually becomes clear and expansive, and the Great Mind immediately arises; therefore, it is said that "one achieves the great resolve."
From "When about to pass away" onwards is the second section, the formal entrustment of the household legacy.
This is further divided into two parts:
first, the entrustment of the legacy; second, the expression of joy.
The first section has four parts:

first, the time of entrusting the task; second, commanding the son to assemble the multitude as witnesses; third, the formal reunion of father and son; and fourth, the actual entrustment of the family estate.

Initially, at the time of entrustment, when he was about to pass away, this was the clear moment of the season; it was the time when his transformative conditions were nearing their end, eight years after preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Vulture Peak, as he proclaimed his entry into *nirvāṇa*.

"Then he commanded his sons": this marks the second section, the gathering of the assembly. These are the disciples transformed by twenty trillion Buddhas, whom he calls "sons"; it refers to those of great capacity whose faculties have matured, gathering from the ten directions like clouds.
The phrase "surrounded by the fourfold assembly above" refers to this.

Regarding the expression "assembling his kinsmen," the old commentary states that the emanated bodies are like kinsmen; the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) is like a king, the ninth stage like a great minister, the eighth stage like a *kṣatriya*, and the seventh stage like a householder.

In the northern lands, they use the *vibhajya-bhūmi* as their kinsmen, the *prabhākari-bhūmi* as their kings, the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) as their ministers, the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) as their *kṣatriyas*, and the thirty minds of the preparatory stages (*triṃśad-āśaya-citta*) as their householders.

If this is so, since the Dharma was being preached during the section on the traces (the *迹门*) and neither the divided bodies nor Prabhūtaratna had yet appeared before them, how could he point to them?

Their explanation is as follows: it was precisely at the time when Śāriputra harbored doubts and had not yet been able to give rise to faith within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, that Prabhūtaratna and the divided bodies arrived simultaneously to provide testimony.

If one wonders what further purpose the appearance of Prabhūtaratna serves after doubts have been removed through faith and understanding, and the bestowal of predictions has already been completed, it should be known that Prabhūtaratna had already emerged at the time of the Dharma-exposition;
however, because the scribe did not wish to repeat the same passage, he placed his appearance later, following the section on the causes for the sequential arrangement.
Now, it is said that this is merely human sentiment and provides no basis for authoritative proof.

When discussing the proximate matters of the Trace Gate (*jimen*), one does not yet employ ancient proofs; however, when discussing the remote matters of the Origin Gate (*benmen*), one must first provide proof from the past.
Now, we do not rely on that interpretation; rather, according to the *Sāyún Sūtra* and other texts, it is explained as follows:

those who are the "influences and echoes" (*yingxiang*) of the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas of the ten directions serve as their kinsmen. These multitudes of influences and echoes were for the most part the former associates (*sahāya*) of Śākyamuni; they all together underwent transformation and edification by the Tathāgata at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas. Since they all stood toward him in the relationship of uncles and cousins, they are thus taken as kinsmen.

Regarding the "King of the Nation" (國王者): among all the gradual and sudden sutras, there is none that does not designate the locus of its primary teaching as the "King of Sutras. Because they benefit sentient beings according to their capacities and because their periods of flourishing and decline occur at different times, each distinct collection is termed a "nation" (國); it is said that being foremost is what constitutes a "king" (王).
Furthermore, this sutra harmonizes all teachings; is it not, therefore, a gathering of the kings? Thus, it was already collected therein in the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, which states:

"First, the Four Truths and the twelvefold dependent origination were taught; next, the Vaipulya sūtras of the twelve divisions were taught; and subsequently, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Avataṃsaka, and the ocean-like emptiness were taught. This refers to the universal collection of all sūtras, wherein the gradual and sudden teachings are integrated and unified within this scripture; hence, it is called the "Gathering of the Kings."
Maitreya and the other great Bodhisattvas are all those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) who serve as ministers.
From the first to the ninth bhūmi, they are Kṣatriyas, born into the lineage of the Dharma Kings.
Those with thirty minds of resolve are householders.
All of these have been transformed by Śākyamuni.
From the words "You gentlemen should know" onwards is the third section, which brings together the father and sons.
"He has indeed received instruction from me; he is truly my son.
He has gained understanding through me; he is born of me.
I have indeed taught the Great Dharma in the presence of twenty trillion buddhas; therefore, I am truly his father."

Regarding the phrase "in a certain city," this scripture contains many names of countries in the texts of the Western Regions (India), while those transmitted here [to China] are very few; perhaps it was possible to state the ancient names of the countries as in the *Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū* parable, but now the names are abbreviated and one simply says "a certain place."

These sentient beings turn their backs on this Mahāyāna, giving rise to the darkness of ignorance and fleeing into the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is said that they "abandoned me and ran away.
Having fully experienced the six realms of existence, it is said that they have been gone for "more than fifty years."
