"Formerly, while in his native city, he harbored anxiety and sought [his son]" means that from of old, within the stage of the Dharma-body, he has constantly used the two types of wisdom to observe and seek out those with the capacity for transformation.
Beginning from this very day, the Way of resonance has been mutually attained; hence it is said, "Suddenly, in this very moment, I have encountered him.
From the words "Now that which I possess" onwards is the fourth section, the formal entrustment of the family business.
"All that exists" refers to all the myriad practices and myriad virtues of the Mahāyāna; hence the phrase "all that exists.

Regarding the statement, "What was previously brought forth and internalized is what the son knows," this is a retrospective reference to the extensive and abbreviated *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings entrusted during the former period of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, including both common and uncommon dharmas. These are what you know, and thus they are what you possess. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), rather than further elaborating on all the various aspects of practice.

"From 'The impoverished son heard these words of his father' onwards is the second section: Receiving the Entrustment with Joy. This refers to receiving the aforementioned great vehicles and experiencing what was never before attained. Previously, he had no aspiration for the Buddha-way; yet now, suddenly hearing that he has received the prediction of Buddhahood, it is said that he has obtained it without seeking."

In the Tripiṭaka, one does not seek because the fundamental mind does not so desire; in the Vaipulya, one does not seek because one feels ashamed of the Lesser Vehicle and all hope for it has been severed; in the Prajñāpāramitā, although one understands that it is not within one's own lot, one still does not seek. Thus, through such non-seeking, it is now spontaneously attained.
From "The World-Honored One, the Great Rich Householder" onwards is the second section, the application of the parable.
Guangzhai’s application of it is sometimes before and sometimes after [the text], and his explanation is extremely brief.
Now, I shall merely point out the underlying meaning according to the text and will not elaborate further on each detail.
As for the synthesis of the parables, the priority lies in grasping the essential meaning rather than exhausting oneself with prolixity.
"The great wealthy elder" corresponds to the parable of the father and son who lost each other.

The analogy consists of four parts; however, by combining the father and son, the remaining meanings are collectively obtained. In this analogy, the Tathāgata corresponds to the father, while "semblance" (sì) corresponds to the son.
There are two senses to this "semblance":

first, taking those of great capacity as the sons; since they previously fled and have not yet attained the true stage, they still abide among the external ordinary beings (bālapṛthagjana), and thus they are called "semblances."
Regarding the taking of a person of lesser capacity as a son: this refers to one whose lesser capacity merely resembles the root-nature of the Mahāyāna.
Since the son has fled from his father, he is disparaged with words such as these.
Question:
The initial commentary on the chapter states: "Having already attained entry into the True," why then does it here say "resembling"?
Answer:
This refers to the time when the child flees from the father; therefore, it is said to be "resembling."
At the beginning of this chapter, when it clarifies the time the son attained enlightenment, your question was incorrect.

From the passage "The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons" onwards, it corresponds to the analogy of the father and son meeting; however, it only corresponds to the elder seeing the son and immediately recognizing him.

From the passage beginning with "Because we [suffer] from the three types of suffering" onwards, the combined exhortation and invitation parallels the two types of inducement mentioned above—the lateral and the sequential; here too, there are now two.
Above, first the lateral was sent away and then sequentially pursued, followed by being abandoned;
now, the lack of capacity for both methods is combined.
"To be caught by [wrong] views yet think to oneself that one is without fault" indicates a lack of great capacity;
"delighting in and clinging to minor dharmas" indicates that while there is small resolve, it is not appropriate to abandon them.
“Today the World-Honored One has caused us... and below, these two inducements and parables are combined.
Above, there was a separate teaching that explored and led [the disciples]; now, the two meanings are unified.
From “Having eliminated... and below, the separate teaching is combined, fully recounting the matters mentioned above.
From "We shall apply ourselves with diligent effort therein" onwards, this corresponds to the previous section on seeking and clearing away the filth.
From "Attaining [the state of] Nirvana" onwards, this corresponds to the previous section on first taking the price.

From the passage beginning with "However, the World-Honored One first knew us," the previous section on the introduction is now summarized. Of the four analogies in the preceding section, three are now summarized here; the analogy of the formal teaching is not summarized separately, as it is already encompassed by the aforementioned diligent effort in removing dung, and thus is not summarized again.
Previously it was said that she saw him from afar; now it is said that she knew of him beforehand.
Previously it was said that she was emaciated and haggard; now it is said that her mind was attached to base desires.

Previously it was said that she immediately cast off her jeweled necklace and put on coarse, tattered clothes; now it is said that she simply abandoned them without making any distinction regarding her precious treasures.
From the passage "By the power of skillful means, he speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom" onwards, the analogy of entrusting the family estate is combined;
above, there was both the reason and the entrustment, and now the combination likewise consists of two parts.
It is twofold:
first, placing one's trust; second, entrusting one's affairs.
Now, when combined, there are likewise two.
First, there are two kinds of faith.
First is "faith in the identity of essence.

Regarding the phrase "expounding the Tathāgata’s wisdom through the power of skillful means," the older tradition states that the cause of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is maintained as the fruit of the Two Vehicles.

Now it is clarified that, while employing the expedient means (*upāya*) of the three vehicles, he teaches the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is said: "By the power of expedient means, he preaches the Mahāyāna dharma before us.

This also harmonizes the ease of both entering and emerging: by the power of expedient means he emerges to distinguish the two vehicles, and by the power of the Buddha’s wisdom he enters to clarify the true reality.
If you do not embody this faith, how could you clarify the Buddha’s wisdom before me?
From the passage "We have obtained from the Buddha the price of one day's wages for nirvana" onwards, the text remains joined as it was in its original place.
From the passage "We also, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom" onwards, they collectively inherit the family estate.
Above, there was both the command and the acceptance; now, they simply accept it collectively.
There are four ways of accepting:
First, receiving the mandate; second, having no desire for gain; third, not abandoning the lowly; fourth, gradually attaining ease and expansiveness. Now, only two are combined.
In the first [section], "receiving the mandate" and "undertaking the task" are combined.
The passage beginning with "And yet, within this" combines the absence of seeking with the attainment of all things.
"Having no aspiration" clarifies that the Buddha’s majestic power is added so that one may speak according to the Buddha's own mind; therefore, I have no aspiration.
The section beginning with "Why is this so? explains the meaning of having no aspiration for [attainment].

By the power of skillful means, he speaks according to the minds of those following the Hīnayāna, saying that there is no share [in the Dharma]; because of this, they do not know that they are truly children of the Buddha, and therefore they do not accept it.

Regarding the statement, “The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, speaks according to us,” this means that the Buddha, endowed with the power of skillful means, teaches the Dharma of true reality (dharmatā) in common with those of the Two Vehicles. Because we do not recognize his intention regarding what is not shared [with them], we are not true sons of the Buddha.
"From 'Now we have finally come to know' below, [the section] on entrusting the family business has two parts:
the act of entrustment and the expression of joy."
Now, the combination also consists of two parts.
Regarding the four types of entrustment of karma mentioned above, they are now combined and entrusted as a whole.
There are two kinds of entrustment:
First, it clarifies that the Buddha is fundamentally without parsimony;
second, it explains that his lack of parsimony is precisely because [beings] delight in the Lesser Vehicle and were not yet ready for the Great Vehicle.

Within this sutra, the later section cites the present to verify the past: since the principle of the present is one and only, we know that the three vehicles of the past were not ultimate. It was merely because they were not yet capable that he disparaged the Lesser Mind prior to the Great. His intent was to cause them to abandon the false and grasp the true; thus, one certainly knows it was not out of parsimony, for the Buddha truly teaches and transforms beings through the Mahāyāna.
"From 'We say that originally there was no mind' onwards, it harmonizes with joy; this is also the meaning of the threefold lack of seeking.
Of the eighty-six and a half verses, the first seventy-three and a half verses praise what precedes;
the subsequent thirteen verses extol the profound depth of the Buddha's grace."
The first part also has two sections:
the first two lines verse the Dharma-explanation (dharmadeśanā),
while the subsequent seventy-one and a half lines verse the parable-explanation (aupamyadeśanā).
In the prose exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), the "seeking" is not praised, but rather the "attainment by oneself" is praised.
Furthermore, the praise of the parable has two parts:
the first forty-one verses praise the opening of the parable;
The following thirty and a half verses summarize the preceding parables.
The first section contained four parts:
the father and son losing each other, their meeting, the entrusting of the business, and the handing over of the wealth; all of these are now summarized in verse.
The first thirteen lines eulogize the loss of father and son. Regarding the four analogies for this mutual loss:
first, the son turns his back on his father; second, the father seeks his son; third, the son gradually returns; and fourth, the father longs for his son.
Now, these verses also consist of four parts, though they do not follow the sequential order.
First, one and a half lines correspond to the first [section], "The Son Leaves His Father";
next, seven lines correspond to the second, "The Father Seeks the Son but Does Not Find Him."
Next, the third [section] consists of two lines, which by way of an interlinear verse (chao-song) further deepens the sorrowful reflection of the fourth;
next, the fourth [section] consists of two and a half lines, which by way of a retrospective verse (zhui-song) describes the gradual return toward the father as described in the third.
The four preceding sections each contain two [verses].

Now, for the first: the one and a half lines beginning with "For example" (譬) only versify the son turning his back on his father and departing; they do not versify his journey toward the kingdom and his subsequent return.

In the "Burning House" parable, the term "kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages" refers broadly to the domains ruled by the elder; here, however, it clarifies that the "various kingdoms" are the three realms of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) experienced by the impoverished son, while the "fifty-odd years" refer to the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
"His father grieves and ponders" marks the second section; these seven lines are a verse on the father’s failure to find his son.
As there were two parts above, there are likewise two parts here in the verse.
The first half-verse praises the failure to find the son.
The following six and a half verses, beginning with "Having grown weary from seeking him," praise the fact that he did not abandon his household affairs because of the loss of one son.

Regarding "seeking in the four directions," this differs from the preceding section. In the former case, the four directions refer to reasoning based on the Four Noble Truths; in the present case, the four directions refer to observing the four modes of birth to seek out sentient beings who are suitable vessels for deliverance.

"Building a house" refers to the *parinirvāṇa* with remainder in other lands; it means establishing the house of compassion and relying upon the dwelling of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
"A great multitude coming and going" refers to the bodhisattvas from various lands coming and going to hear the Dharma.
Regarding the passage "and my years have grown old," this third section consists of two lines that skip ahead to summarize the fourth [section], wherein his sorrowful anxiety deepens.

The preceding text contained two parts; here, however, it merely summarizes his prior loss of his son and his current suffering at having no one to whom he can entrust [his lineage], which is why he grieves.

"Then the impoverished son sought food and clothing," and so forth; this is the fourth section, consisting of two and a half lines, which reiterates the third section above—the gradual return toward the father.
The preceding prose text contained two parts, and the present verse likewise contains two.
The first two lines of the verse praise the reason for approaching his father: it was because he sought food and clothing.
"Gradually passing through" and so forth, comprising half a line, praises his actual arrival at his father’s city.
Initially, one approaches the father through the middle.

Regarding the phrase "from village to village": the mutual interaction between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is like a "village," while the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are like a "country."
Cultivating contaminated wholesome dharmas is like "having something to grasp. Cultivating the wholesome dharmas of the two vehicles is like "non-attainment.

Not obtaining the Dharma-food of the Mahāyāna is "hunger"; lacking great power and function is "emaciation"; lacking great merit is "leanness"; and giving rise to views and afflictions regarding existence and non-existence is "sores and scabs."
From the seven and a half verses beginning with "Hired laborer," the second section, "Father and Son Meet," is versified.
The preceding prose text contains two parts; the present verse section likewise contains two.
The first six and a half verses versify the son seeing his father.
The next line praises the father seeing his son.
Regarding the previous section on the son seeing the father, there were four textual passages; here, three are praised:
the first half-line praises the cause for seeing the father, which was that he reached his father’s house by means of working as a hired laborer.
Next, from "At that time, the elder... onwards, the second section consisting of two and a half lines praises the third sign: seeing his father.
The previous passage clarified the location where he saw his father; that location was by the side of the gate.
Now, by saying "the elder was within his gate," the specific location is further specified.
The passage beginning with "bestowing a great jeweled canopy" correctly depicts the father’s appearance, seated majestically upon a lion throne.

The Dharma-body is the teacher and the king; the retributive body is the elder. The "notes, records, deeds, and documents" refer to the bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), clarifying the practice of cultivation.

I maintain that expounding the extensive meaning of what is concise constitutes a "commentary" (zhù); bestowing the prediction of enlightenment constitutes a "record" (jì); the four great vows constitute a "contract" (quàn); and spiritual practice constitutes an "annotation" (shū).
The three and a half lines beginning with "The impoverished son saw his father" eulogize the fourth [stage]: the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance.
The one line beginning with "At that time, the elder" eulogizes the second [stage]: the father seeing the son.
The preceding passage contains four sections:
first, the locus of views; second, views as consciousness; third, joy in views; and fourth, the fulfillment of wishes.
Now, only two are versified:
The first half of the verse describes the place where he sees his son;
"seeing him from afar" and below constitutes the second section, one and a half lines, which describes recognizing the son upon seeing him.
"He immediately commands the messengers to pursue and seize him" and below constitutes the third section, ten and a half lines, which parallels the preceding analogy of pursuit and enticement.
Now, for the first part, there are three lines of verse that follow along the side.
Regarding the preceding text that follows along the side of the person, there are three sections:
first, calling the son but he does not come; second, calling him again but he still does not come; third, letting him go.
Now, the first three lines of the verse commemorate the initial call when there was no responsive capacity and [the Buddha] did not come;
next, from "bewildered and distressed" (*mimèn*) downward, the second section consists of one line, commemorating the second call when [he still] did not come;

next, from "this person" (*shìrén*) downward, the third section consists of two lines, commemorating the lack of responsive capacity, which is precisely the aforementioned intent to release and abandon [him].

From "He immediately employs skillful means" (*yījí fāngbiàn*) onwards is the second section, consisting of seven and a half lines, which versifies the secret dispatching of two persons to entice [the son].
The preceding prose text has two parts; the current verse likewise has two.
The first three lines of the verse illustrate the analogy of hiring labor;
the subsequent four and a half lines illustrate the analogy of instructing labor.
Regarding the four aspects of the preceding analogy of hiring labor:
There are four parts: first, employing skillful means; second, obtaining it immediately upon seeking; third, stating the employment of labor; and fourth, taking payment for clearing away filth.
Here, only two are versified:
the first two lines verse the first part, the employment of skillful means.
The line beginning with "When the impoverished son heard this" (the first line of the next verse) praises the fourth stage: accepting wages to remove filth.
Herein, the initial establishment of skillful means is shown: "one-eyed" refers to partial emptiness;
"dwarfed" refers to being short in stature, meaning one has not yet reached the source of the true reality (*dharmatā*).
"Vulgar" means narrow and constricted, lacking the adornment of the manifold virtues of the Mahāyāna.
The absence of the four fearlessnesses is termed "lacking majesty," and the departure from the extraordinary [qualities of] bliss, self, and purity is termed "lacking virtue."

Next, from "The impoverished son heard this" onwards is the second section, "Taking the Price," which refers to the room for purifying the six sense-faculties and the house of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
From "The elder at the window" onwards, the second part consisting of four lines and a half, is a verse summarizing the aforementioned instruction on how to act.
The preceding prose passage consists of four parts, and this verse likewise has four.
The first half-line of the verse corresponds to the section on the window;
the second half-line, beginning with "Thinking of my son's folly and inferiority," corresponds to the section on emaciation.
From "Thereupon the elder put on" below, the third section consists of one line, which praises the discarding of the exquisite for the coarse;
from "Skillfully drawing near" below, the fourth section consists of two and a half lines, which praises the correct teaching and practice.
Above there are seven categories of Dharma gates: "Speech" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
"urging them to diligent practice" refers to the four right efforts;
the line beginning with "Since I have increased your wages" praises the four bases of psychic power.
"Anointing the feet with oil" enables one to walk upon deep water as if by supernormal power; furthermore, oil can eliminate wind, which signifies the absence of distraction.

"Abundant food and drink" refers to superior rice and flour; "thick and warm bedding" refers to the meditative cultivation of contemplation, refinement, and perfuming, which can eliminate discursive movement.

The half-line, "In this way, you should diligently practice these words of exhortation," summarizes the fourth [section] on consolation and the fifth on the absence of the five faults; once the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are perfected, one is then capable of receiving such exhortations.

The half-line, "Furthermore, with gentle words," summarizes the sixth on the act of writing and the seventh on causing them to be practiced constantly; both of these pertain to the stage of being a child (*putrasthāna*).
"‘The elder possesses wisdom’ and below—this is the fourth section, the ten lines, which versifies the fourth [section] above, the entrustment of the family estate.
The preceding prose text has two parts; the present verse likewise has two."
Now, the first three lines and a half of the verse explain the reason for entrusting the karma;
the subsequent six lines and a half constitute the actual entrustment of the karma.
Regarding the initial reason, there are two parts, and the present verse likewise has two.

First, the second half-line of the verse beginning with "The elder was wise" provides a general summary of the mind’s characteristics and its embodiment of faith, which constitutes the entry and exit;
the second section, consisting of three lines beginning with "After twenty years," summarizes the detailed assumption of the family business.
In the preceding section, there was mention of karma, existence, life-force, and sensation; here, however, we only recite the verse on sensation and life-force.
In the preceding section, there were four types of sensation and life-force, whereas here we only recite three.
The first one and a half lines of the verse recite the sensation and life-force.
Next, from "still remaining at the gate" onwards is the second section, one line, which praises [the son] still occupying his original position and not yet having abandoned his inferior mind;
next, from "the father knowing the son's mind" onwards is the third section, half a line, which praises the awakening of the Mahāyāna faculty through the vast ambition of universal ease.

First, regarding the "twenty years": this cannot be equated with the previous case where the removal of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions of views) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions of cultivation) was termed "twenty. Here, it clarifies the attachment to worldly affairs.

Alternatively, it is said that by turning the Mahāyāna teachings to instruct all bodhisattvas, one cuts off the distinct delusions of Mahāyāna—namely, both *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya*—and this is termed "twenty years."
Some say that the period of his teaching the Prajñāpāramitā lasted for twenty years.
Others say that the twenty years were spent while he resided in the stages of the Two Vehicles, turning the Mahāyāna teachings.
The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "In the twenty-eighth year, he preached the Mahāprajñā.

From the passage beginning with "Wishing to bestow wealth and goods" onwards, the second section consists of six and a half lines of verse, which constitutes the second part: the formal entrustment of the family estate.
The preceding prose consists of two parts, and the present verse likewise has two.
The first four and a half lines of verse correspond to the formal entrustment of the task;
the subsequent two lines correspond to the joy of having received the entrustment.
Regarding the four types of formal entrustment of affairs mentioned above, only three are now versified here, as there is no [entrustment] regarding time.
The first line, beginning with "desiring to give," versifies the second [section] above: gathering one's kinsmen.
"Regarding 'In this great assembly' below," the second section consists of two and a half lines, which versify the third point above: the natural relationship between father and son.
"Regarding 'Whatever I possess' below," the third section consists of one line, which versifies the fourth point above: the formal entrustment.
"Recalling my former poverty," and so forth, is the second section; these two lines of verse praise the joy of receiving [the teaching].
"The Buddha is also like this," and so forth, consists of three and a half verses; these verses correspond to the parable.

"The Buddha is also like this" corresponds to the first analogy of the father and son losing each other; "knowing that I delight in the small" corresponds to the analogy of the father and son meeting; and the two lines beginning with "never before having spoken" correspond to the third analogy of the pursuit and summons.
There are two types of "upper conjunctions" (*ūrdhvasaṃyoga*):
first, the conjunction where one does not return despite being called again; second, the conjunction of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*).
This verse now summarizes their meaning in general.
The line beginning with "And says to us" (而說我等) is a verse summarizing the preceding analogy of sending two people in secret to entice [the fish].
This summarizes the two preceding chapters on the "Teaching of Equalization" (齊教) and the "Probing Teaching" (探教); this current line merely summarizes their general meaning.
From "The Buddha charged us" below, there are twenty-eight and a half lines; these verses correspond to the fourth section, Receiving the Family Business. This section consists of two parts:
establishing trust and entrusting the business. Of these, the first eighteen and a half lines only correspond to the entrustment of the business;
the subsequent ten lines correspond to the formal entrustment itself.
Regarding the superior reception of the mandate, there are only two aspects:
first, the reception of the mandate; second, the absence of seeking or grasping.
Now, the first line of the long verse introduces the reception of the mandate, while the subsequent lines introduce what is absent.
"The Supreme Path" is precisely the emptiness of *prajñā*, for there is nothing superior to it.
The following seventeen and a half lines correctly receive the entrustment of life and the absence of seeking, as well as the state of non-relinquishment and thorough composure.
The five lines beginning with "I receive the Buddha's teaching" constitute the verse for formally accepting the mandate.
That "the sons of the Buddha hear the Dharma and attain realization" clarifies the transmission of the teaching to benefit others.
At that time, it is said that he turns the teaching; he transforms and educates bodhisattvas without speaking of them as "mine.

The passage beginning with "Like that impoverished son," spanning twelve and a half lines, praises the second [quality], the absence of seeking or grasping; this text is an extensive elaboration upon the above.
Within this, there are again two parts:

first, one line, which restates the preceding analogy and applies it; second, from "Although we speak" onwards, eleven and a half lines, which properly apply the principle of having no desire for gain, further divided into three:
the first line, which directly versifies having no desire for gain.

Next, the nine and a half lines beginning with "We have attained internal cessation" consist of both wisdom and abandonment, and thus are free from longing or grasping; furthermore, they are divided into three parts:
the thesis, the explanation, and the conclusion.
The first part consists of two sections:
first, one line which indicates that because they possess the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), there is no seeking or grasping;
second, from "If we were to hear... onwards, the next line which indicates that because they possess the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), there is no seeking or grasping.
The six lines beginning with "Why is this so? provide a dual explanation of the two chapters on wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Next, the one and a half lines beginning with "Although we... constitute the third section, which concludes by explaining that they themselves have no desire for acquisition.

Next, following "The Teacher’s Vision," the third section consists of one line, clarifying that the Buddha perceives my abandonment [of the teaching] and thus it is appropriate that I have no desire to receive it.
Following "Like a Wealthy Elder," the next ten lines are a verse on the formal entrustment of the task.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the formal entrustment of the task; second, the joy of having received the entrustment.
The present verse likewise consists of two parts:
The first three lines of the verse praise the formal entrustment (*samyak-parindanā*);
the subsequent seven lines praise the attainment of joy.

Within the first three lines, the former [section] generally synthesizes the activity of the formal entrustment, while the present [verse] likewise provides a general summary. Specifically, the first one and a half lines cite the analogy and apply it to the subject matter, while the following one and a half lines formally summarize the synthesis.
The seven lines beginning with "We, this very day" eulogize the second [point]: attaining joy upon receiving the entrustment.
"Attaining the Way" means attaining the Way of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Attaining the fruit" means partially attaining the habitual fruits of the Mahāyāna.
These two phrases clarify the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge.
"Obtaining the pure eye regarding untainted dharmas" means these two phrases clarify the opening of the Buddha’s vision, seeing the principle of the true mark (lakṣaṇa).
In the past, seeing the outflow-free (anāsrava) meant not falling into the state of an ordinary person; today, seeing the outflow-free means not falling into the state of the Two Vehicles.
In the past, the eye of wisdom saw emptiness; now, the pure eye sees the Middle Way.

Regarding "the retribution of upholding the precepts": in the past, one practiced the pure conduct of the precepts together with the manifestation of the outflow-free state; yet, when the body was reduced to ashes and wisdom extinguished, there was no person to receive this fruit-retribution. Today, through pure conduct, one is able to attain the outflow-free state—this is the meaning of the "revealing cause" (了因) taking its fruit. Upholding the precepts is the meaning of the "conditioning cause" (緣因), and the principle perceived by the pure eye is the meaning of the "true cause" (正因).
Those who say, "We are truly śrāvakas," are those at the true stage of the Mahāyāna.

During the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), although one voice pervades the trichiliocosm, this is a semblance of the Path rather than the true; upon entering the ten abodes (*vihāra*), it becomes the true.
A true Arhat possesses three meanings; here, only the single meaning of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat) is cited.

If one does not undergo transformation-death and slays both the general and specific delusions, this constitutes the meaning of "Non-arising" and "Slayer of Thieves. Being capable of serving as a field of merit for the ten dharma-realms is the meaning of "Worthy of Offerings. Thus, "Worthy of Offerings" and "Slayer of Thieves" mutually illuminate one another.
The following thirteen lines praise the Buddha’s profound kindness as being difficult to repay, as the text states.

I privately comment that "the Great Kindness of the World-Honored One" refers to: first, the Buddha’s initial establishment of compassion, whereby he uproots the suffering of the six realms and bestows the bliss of the four noble stages; he universally encompasses the ten dharma realms within the Four Great Vows—this is the kindness of the Tathāgata’s Sanctuary.

Second, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he instructed, taught, benefited, and gladdened me; he once taught me the Mahāyāna, and although I have since forgotten it, my wisdom and vows have not been lost. Indeed, the Tathāgata’s dwelling is cool and warm; his great compassion bestows happiness—this is his grace.

Third, when sentient beings encounter suffering, they regard [the Buddha] merely as a father; yet the Buddha observes their needs as a calf follows its mother. He fully practices the six perfections to benefit sentient beings, for the Tathāgata’s dwelling wards off the cold and obstructs the heat, and his great compassion uproots suffering—this is his grace.

Fourth, after attaining enlightenment, the Buddha ought to enjoy the bliss of unconditioned quiescence; yet he concealed his divine virtues and employed the Dharma of the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Actions, which the poor delight in, sprinkling cold water upon their faces to bring them to awakening—this is indeed the grace of the Buddha’s robe shielding them from the heat of greed and desire.

Fifth, he manifested the appearance of an aged bhikṣu and used skillful means to approach him, giving him the price of a single day’s labor; this was the grace of the Buddha’s robe that removed the sight of cold and provided relief from heat.

Sixth, after this had passed, he inspired mutual trust through his demeanor and then rebuked and disparaged him, causing him to feel shame for his smallness and aspire toward greatness; this was the grace of the Buddha’s robe that concealed his ugliness.
Seventh, he entrusted me with the family business, making me fully acquainted with all the gold, silver, and treasuries; this was due to the grace of the Buddha’s robe and its adornment of me.

Eighth, he assembled my kinsmen, established the relationship between father and son, and handed over the family estate; that the unsurpassed mass of jewels was obtained without seeking was due to the grace of the Tathāgata’s seat.

9. Having sat upon the seat, my body and mind became serene and I attained profound peace and stability. By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, I cause all to hear; among all devas and humans, I am universally worthy of receiving offerings. This Tathāgata’s seat enables me to be fully endowed with the grace of self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
This refers to what is meant by the saying: "The great kindness of the World-Honored One cannot be repaid, even if one were to carry it upon both shoulders.
*The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Six, Part Two.
